title: Slope & Gradient Calculator: Percent and Angle
description: Convert rise and run into percent grade, angle and ratio with the Slope & Gradient Calculator — all three dialects of steepness at once. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a rise of 3 feet over a 40-foot run is a 7.5% grade, a 4.29° angle and a 1 : 13.3 ratio — one slope, three correct ways to say it.
quick_answer: The Slope & Gradient Calculator converts a rise and a run into the three standard ways of stating steepness: percent grade, slope angle in degrees, and rise-over-run ratio. Enter the two measurements in any matching unit and read all three — no translating between road crews, architects and trig tables.
steps_intro: Two measurements in, every dialect of steepness out:

body.t: Roofers speak in pitch (rise per 12 of run): a 6-in-12 roof is a 50% grade and a 26.57° angle. This is the translator between the roof and the building code.
Race profiles quote percent; your legs feel angle. Convert a climb's numbers before the ride, and check its true length with the
Drainage specs come as ratios (1 : 80, 1 : 40). Read them as percent and angle here so the fall you dig is the fall the drawing meant.
Swales, banks and accessible paths each carry a target steepness in a different dialect. One conversion up front prevents three phone calls later.
Rise equals run and the slope is 100% grade at exactly 45°. Everything steeper is more rise than run — a fact that makes 'a 200% grade' sound dramatic and a 63.4° slope sound merely technical.

A path rising 1 m over 20 m of run: 5% grade, 2.86°, ratio 1 : 20. Gentle to walk, and right at the edge of what many accessibility guidelines treat as a ramp rather than a path — the number decides which rules apply.

popular_table.intro: Computed (angle = atan(rise ÷ run)) — pin the row your project speaks.
popular_table.note: Percent and degrees part company as slopes grow: doubling the grade does not double the angle. At small grades they nearly agree, which is exactly why the confusion survives.

faq: How do I convert percent grade to degrees?
Take the arctangent of the grade as a decimal: angle = atan(percent ÷ 100). Ten percent is atan(0.10) = 5.71°. The calculator does it both ways.
What does a 1 : 12 ratio mean in percent?
One unit of rise per twelve of run: 1 ÷ 12 = 8.33%. Ratios divide the other way from how they are often read aloud — 'one in twelve' is rise over run.
Which unit should my rise and run be in?
Any unit, as long as both match — feet with feet, metres with metres. Grade, angle and ratio are unit-free because the units cancel in the division.
Can the run be measured along the slope?
That distance is the slope length, not the run. Using it as the run understates steepness slightly; on a 10% grade the error is about half a percent of the value.
The foot-based trade convention: pitch states inches of rise per 12 inches (one foot) of run. A 4-in-12 pitch is a 33.3% grade at 18.43°.
It records direction — a fall rather than a rise. Drainage and road profiles use the sign; the steepness magnitude is identical.
What is the steepest this can express?
As the run approaches zero the grade runs to infinity and the angle to 90°. Vertical faces are the limit the mathematics points at but roads never reach.
